en: Prosperity!
The Experience of Non-duality
I am Śiva alone, characterized by bliss, truth, and so forth;
because my nature is eternal bliss and the like, I am immovable and non-dual. 1.1.
Just as the single moon appears as two due to a defect in the eye, so too the one Self appears falsely as two through the power of māyā. 1.2
Just as there is only one moon for those free from defects of vision, so too is the Self always one for those free from the defect of illusion. 1.3
Duality appears in the moon through a defect of the eye, and the world [appears] through one's own Māyā;
just as duality in the moon is false, so too is duality in the Self false. 1.4
Space cannot exist as an effect without the Self;
since the fullness of the effect is established, how much more so the fullness of the Self? (1.5)
Just as space, which is the effect, is indeed one and not twofold,
so too this Self, which is the cause, is one for the one who knows.
Just as the one ether appears as two due to limiting adjuncts, so too this Self, though one and full, appears as two due to limiting adjuncts. (1.7)
The consciousness conditioned by the cause is not greater than the consciousness residing in the effect;
the space within a jar is never anywhere greater than the space within the clay [from which it was made]. (1.8)
Just as space becomes one when freed from its limiting adjuncts, so too this Self is always one when freed from its limiting adjuncts. 1.9
Just as there is no space other than space, because of its oneness, so too no self other than the Self is established for the Self. 1.10
Just as water, through its association with clouds,
assumes the form of hailstones, so too the Self, through its association with māyā, assumes the form of the phenomenal world.
It appears like a rain-stone (hailstone) due to its association with the cloud, yet it is merely water;
for indeed, there is no destruction of the water itself when the rain-stone perishes. || 1.12 ||
This very Self appears as such through the connection with māyā, like the phenomenal world;
yet, by the destruction of the phenomenal world, there is never any destruction of the Self. 1.13
Just as a bubble arising from water appears as if it were something other than the water, so too this manifold phenomenal world appears as if it were separate from the Self. 1.14
Just as the destruction of a bubble never entails the destruction of water, so too, by the destruction of phenomenal manifestation, there can be no destruction of the Self. 1.15
Just as one born from a non-serpent would not become a serpent even if purified and so forth,
so too one born from the gross and so forth would not attain this [pure state] even if purified and so forth.
Just as a serpent does not regard its cast-off skin as its self, so too the man of knowledge always regards the three bodies that have been abandoned as not being the self. 1.17
Just as the snake is not destroyed by the destruction of its slough, so too there can be no destruction of the Self through the destruction of the three bodies. 1.18

Just as ignorant people [perceive] buttermilk and other substances as being salty when they are mixed with salt, so too the Self, when conjoined with the gross body and its attributes, is defiled by them as if it were the gross body itself. (1.19)
Just as iron, wood, and other such things appear as fire through contact with fire, so too does everything—gross objects and the rest—appear as the Self through its union with its own Self. 1.20
The burner cannot be the burning; likewise, the burning cannot be the burner.
This self cannot be non-self, nor can this non-self be the self. (1.21)
The triad beginning with the object of knowledge, along with its meaning, shines by him as a pot or a wall shines by the sun;
he who shines thus is indeed I, distinct from the object of knowledge and the rest. (1.22)
Just as a jar or other objects appear to shine by virtue of the radiance of the sun, so too do objects of cognition and the like appear to shine by virtue of the radiance of the Self. (1.23)

Just as one becomes full of affection through contact with molasses and the like made from flour, so too, through its connection with the Self, the object of cognition and the rest become full of affection, as it were, like the Self. (1.24)
The heat of water, a jar, or flour arises from contact with fire;
how could they possess heat anywhere without fire? (1.25)
The manifestation of the elements, their derivatives, and the body occurs through union with one's own Self;
for how could they ever have manifestation anywhere without the Self? (1.26)
Just as the one sky dwells within various kinds of jars, so too do I, the One, dwell within various kinds of bodies. 1.27.
Just as the sky does not itself undergo the diversity of various jars, even so do I not undergo the diversity of bodies. (1.28)
Just as when jars are destroyed, the space within the jars is not destroyed, so too, when bodies perish, I, the all-pervading one, am never destroyed. 1.29
Just as flowers, from the finest to the lowest, exist upon a single thread, so too do bodies, from the highest to the lowest, always abide within me.
Just as one thread does not touch the flowers from the best to the lowest,
so too I, the all-pervading, do not touch the bodies from the best to the lowest.
Just as the thread does not perish when those flowers have perished,
so too I do not perish at all, even though these bodies always perish.
Just as the single ray of the sun appears manifold within the various holes of a bedstead's ropes, so too does the omnipresent One appear as many within the various fields (kṣetra). 1.33.
Just as the defects and such situated within the hole of a rope do not touch the sun's rays,
so too may the defects and such situated within the field not touch me, who am all-pervading.
Just as the sunlight does not perish when the holes in the rope are destroyed,
so too I, the all-pervading one, do not perish when the fields are destroyed.
I am not the body, because it is visible and composed of the elements; nor am I the sense organs.
I am not the vital breath (prāṇa), because it is manifold; nor am I the mind (manas), because it is flickering.

I am not the intellect, because it is subject to modification; I am not darkness (tamas), because it is insentient; nor am I the body, senses, and so forth, because they are perishable like a jar or other such objects. (1.37)
Illuminating the body, senses, vital breaths, mind, intellect, and ignorance,
as well as the ego which identifies with them, I shine forth.
This entire world is not the Self because it is an object of the cognition "this";
nor is the ego (ahaṃ) the Self, for it is always the witness of the ego, as seen in states such as deep sleep. (1.39)
Just as I am without modification during sleep, so too I am in the other two states;
yet, through the application of the two measures, I appear as if modified.
Just as a crystal is not at all stained by adjuncts such as blue or red, so too the Self is not at all stained by any of the desires and other qualities born of the sheaths. 1.41
Just as the earth seems to spin when a plough is being turned,
so too the self, though motionless, appears to move to one who is deluded.
As long as one constantly identifies these three bodies as the self, for that long this deluded person is born in various wombs. 1.43
The sleep, bodily fatigue, suffering, and so forth of the dreaming body do not touch the waking body; likewise, the waking body’s fatigue, suffering, and so forth do not touch the Self. (1.44)
The sleeping body appears like the waking body due to sleep;
yet, with the destruction of the sleeping body, the waking body does not perish. (1.45)
Likewise, this Self appears as the waking body due to the state of waking;
yet, with the destruction of the waking body, the Self is never destroyed. (1.46)
Having abandoned this dream-body, it seeks the waking body;
and just as this [dreamer], awakened from the waking body, abandons itself, so too [does the Self]. (1.47)
Just as one who has awakened no longer has any desire for the enjoyments experienced in a dream, so too the man of knowledge has no desire for unreal enjoyments such as heaven and the like. 1.48

Just as an enjoyer imagines an object of enjoyment externally, such as a snake on a stone, so too do form, character, and other qualities—which are the enjoyments of the self—possess the nature of objects of enjoyment. (1.49)

For the knower, there is no such thing as saṃsāra, just as for the ignorant person who performs ritual actions; there is no fear for one who knows, just as there is none for one who perceives a rope-snake [as merely a rope]. 1.50
Just as a solid block of rock salt becomes water through contact with water,
so too, for those who know Brahman, the intellect becomes the Self itself through union with its own essence.
Just as the sun, though one, appears as many in all its watery receptacles, so too the Self, though one, appears as many in all the fields. (1.52)
Just as the reflection of the sun appears in water as if it were other than the sun itself, so too does the reflection of the Self appear in the intellect as if it were other than the Self. 1.53
Just as without an object there could be no reflection in water, so too, without a self, how could there be an appearance of consciousness in the intellect? (1.54)
Just as flickeringness and other such qualities of a reflection never belong to the original object, so too agency and other such qualities do not belong to the Self. (1.55)

Just as coolness and other qualities in water do not touch the reflection of the sun in the water, so too the actions and other attributes of the intellect do not touch the reflection of consciousness. 1.56

The reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), joined with the intellect's [attributes] such as agency, enjoyership, and suffering, appears as if subject to modification, like the sun reflected in water within a vessel. (1.57)
When the water in a vessel is lost, the sun situated therein appears as if it has perished;
likewise, upon the dissolution of the intellect, this [Self] appears as if lost during sleep.
Just as the sun shines, illuminating the sun reflected in water, the water, and the waves, so too does this [Self] shine,
illuminating the intellect (dhī), which is the reflection of the Self, and the agency and other attributes of the intellect (buddhi).
Just as the sun, which illuminates the clouds, shines even when covered by clouds,
so too does this Self, which illuminates delusion, shine even when shrouded by delusion.

Just as the sun appears shining while illuminating its objects of illumination such as clouds and the like, so too does this [Self] appear shining while illuminating its objects of illumination such as gross bodies and the like. (1.61)
The sun, which illuminates everything, is not defiled by the things it illuminates;
likewise, the Self, which illuminates everything, is not defiled by anything. 1.62
Just as a face situated in a mirror appears falsely as if it were the actual face, so too the illuminator of appearances residing in the intellect appears falsely as if it were the Self. (1.63)
How could the destruction of the face occur through the destruction of its reflection in a mirror?
Through the destruction of the appearance residing in the intellect, there is never any destruction of the Self. (1.64)
Just as a deity fashioned from copper appears as if it were something other than the copper,
so too does this world, arising from the Self, appear in the form of a manifestation and so forth.
Just as copper, though it is one, appears as both the Lord and the individual soul, so too this Self, though it is one, is falsely perceived as the Lord, the individual soul, and so forth. (1.66)
Just as there is no destruction of copper through the destruction of God and so forth, so too there is never any destruction of the self through the destruction of God and so forth. (1.67)
Just as this snake superimposed upon a rope appears as real through the reality of the rope,
so too does this world appear as real through the reality of one's own Self.
Just as by the absence of the superimposed snake only the rope remains, so too by the absence of the world only the Reality that is the Self remains. (1.69)
Just as redness appears in a crystal due to an external adjunct, or blueness in the sky, so does this world appear as if real within the non-dual [reality]. (1.70)
Just as redness in crystal is false and blueness in the sky is a delusion, so too this world is false within me, who am one and non-dual. (1.71)
The person of deluded intellect perceives difference through such states as the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara);
but how could there be any difference in this which is indeed non-dual and devoid of distinctions? (1.72)
By the mere wearing of the liṅga, this Śiva enters into the state of being alive;
if the liṅga is destroyed, how can there be an entry into the state of life for this Śiva? (1.73)
Śiva alone is always the individual soul (jīva), and the individual soul is always Śiva;
he who knows the unity of these two is a knower of the Self, and no other.
Just as water, through its union with milk, falsely appears as milk,
so too this non-self, through its union with the Self, appears as if it were the Self.
Just as a swan becomes [itself] by separating milk from water and not otherwise, so one becomes liberated by separating the Self from the gross body and the rest, and not otherwise. (1.76)
Only the swan, and no other, knows how to distinguish milk from water;
only the ascetic, and no other, knows how to distinguish the Self from the non-Self. (1.77)
Indeed, a transformation of a post superimposed as a thief never occurs anywhere;
likewise, there can be no transformation of the changeless Self arising as the universe.
When the post is known [to be what it is], where is the thief? In the absence of a thief, whence fear?
When the Self is known, where is the universe? In the absence of the universe, whence all things? (1.79)
The three functions of the qualities appear as mutually distinct;
yet that in which their true nature resides is I alone, partless. (1.80)
In that Supreme Brahman, O virtuous one, these three bodies appear;
I am indeed that very Supreme Brahman, distinct from the three bodies.
In that inner Self (pratyagātman) in which the triad beginning with waking exists as if it were real, I am that very Supreme Brahman, distinct from waking and the other states. 1.82.
In that Supreme Self in whom the triad beginning with Viśva exists as reality, I am that very Supreme Self, distinct from Viśva and the others. (1.83)
In that Witness, as if in truth, the triad beginning with Virāṭ shines;
I am that very one, self-luminous, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss. 1.84.
Thus [ends] the work of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya).
The experience of non-duality is complete.
